painted. A graph opens at whatever scale the fit picks, and that scale falls as the graph
grows: past a few hundred nodes the opening frame is text nobody can read, drawn over the
graph it is naming.

ba5b0bde30bb87f79b20d752.source:
`render.minLabelFontSize` is the rendered size, in CSS pixels, below which a label is not
drawn. It defaults to `9`.

71a09b9b45551b9d2a9a65d1.source:
The test is `fontSize × zoom`, in rendered pixels rather than the zoom scale: a scale
multiplies coordinates the layout invented, so the same value means a different apparent size
on the next dataset.

30b90cb54c26b87592e040ca.source:
It is one number for the whole canvas, edge labels and node labels alike. The difference
between them is already in the font size: an edge label is drawn at
`defaultLabelStyle.fontSize` (12 by default), while a node's is derived from the node,
`max(12, size × 0.45)`, so a large node keeps its label to a lower zoom than a small one.
A node style's `textFontSize` replaces that derived size.

56d8d9771a9c0ae1a1b0e329.source: `0` turns the gate off and draws every label at every zoom.

2f1487a0f6c655ea8a452ab0.source:
The text the library places: an edge's `label`, a node's `text`, and whatever
`render.renderLabel` returns. A node's `html`, `renderNode` or tier card is its *drawing*,
and [`tiers`](#node-tiers) is what chooses between drawings.

80a0cf3723f1ee94e30a200e.source:
A label that is showing holds until its rendered size falls to 85% of the threshold, so a
view parked on the line settles instead of flickering. Every label drawn at one size answers
together, whichever element it belongs to.

5d1fbbedf066d67eefc2b045.source:
An edge selected **on its own** shows its label whatever the zoom, counter-scaled so it is
readable rather than the two pixels it was hidden at. An edge has no tooltip and no panel, so
its label is the only thing that answers "what is this". A node needs none of that: it
already answers through its tooltip, the sidebar, and its `focusTier` drawing.

3a079034ec3360486c69a722.source:
A hidden label is not merely invisible, it is not in the graph — which is where the cost goes.
A label is repositioned on every simulation tick, and on a large graph that pass alone costs
more than a frame. What remains after the gate is the stroke, which is cheap.

aebfc7bfb32bca1383987057.source:
Above the threshold, labels can still overlap each other. An edge label is typically wider
than the edge it names, and that ratio does not change with the zoom. This option is about
legibility, not decluttering.

bdc74e452d07df1d3ea1e74d.source:
Pivotick exposes a renderer controller that lets you interact directly with the rendering engine.
All methods are [available online](/api/html/interfaces/GraphRenderer.html)

025bc792e38bbf36d9393deb.source: The rendering method. `'svg'` uses SVG elements, `'canvas'` uses the HTML canvas (experimental - not fully implemented).

b49d01b9cab3d72b2702c3ba.source: Default styling applied to all edges.

c32660545ce64c3838666bd6.source: Default styling applied to all edge labels.

2e002780b477d68f831759d0.source: Custom styles for edge markers (`'arrow'`, `'diamond'`, etc.). See [`MarkerStyle`](/api/html/interfaces/RendererOptions.MarkerStyle.html)

ada25699cb1735aa47d80220.source: The *kind* of an edge, used with `edgeStyleMap` and as a [layer](/edge-layers) key.

ea1c37a318f3c9d8ff24ee48.source: Maps edge kinds (from `edgeTypeAccessor`) to styles. See [Edge layers](/edge-layers).

e579911dbe7b1d1e28a30888.source: The lowest zoom a fit goes to. A graph too big to fit at it opens at this zoom, centred on `fitAnchor`, and the minimap shows the rest.

cc45921b05002dd6a5755916.source: Id of the node a fit held at `minFitScale` centres on. The view stops at the graph's edges, so an anchor on one side stays near that side.

935e2c528e27572c8a95f8dd.source: Enable zoom. `false` also takes the viewport rail's zoom buttons, keeping fit-and-center.

7a8fbb939b8a6ed157cfe765.source: Region selection: `enabled: false` drops the drag marquee **and** the Select ▸ Lasso tool.

bd12492e34101480327b10bf.source: Expanding a cluster: `false` takes the chevron, the `Enter` shortcut and the dashed collapsed outline with it. A selected child still lights its closed cluster.

18642b80978d3861d613f6b1.source: Your card is measured, whatever shape it is

26b000ef41deeba67fc96479.source: `defaultNodeStyle`, `nodeStyleMap[type]`, a node's own style, a `styleCb` return

eeae6b24ba0307a7d63621bf.source: every node, ahead of the styling chain

939ccae405054cf3a9804911.source: What a card does *not* switch off

66e010c126e797bd4b217d01.source:
Pivotick runs entirely in the browser: there is no server, no session and no persistence of its
own. The boundary that matters is the one between **your graph data** and **your page's DOM** —
Pivotick renders the data you hand it into the document your application owns.

3ce6328d580fdc07df38d3b7.source:
If that data comes from somewhere you don't fully control — a threat-intel feed, a CVE mirror, an
imported dataset, another user's upload — treat it as untrusted, and read the rest of this page.

295ae5865e274838f946febf.source:
Everything the library renders from your data is inserted as **text**, not markup. That covers
node and edge labels, descriptions, ids, property keys and values, and note content:

b2ad909c3f484fd3553dac92.source: Labels, descriptions and property names/values are written with `textContent`.

23e6e2b6a3c3b628c20fd27d.source:
Note content is Markdown, rendered with `marked` and then sanitized with
[DOMPurify](https://github.com/cure53/DOMPurify) against an allow-list of the tags Markdown
itself produces. `<style>`, the form elements and inline `style` attributes are not on it.

9ad83dd8e941e270d19b6146.source:
`style.svgIcon` markup is sanitized (SVG profile) before it reaches the document, so event
handlers, `<script>` and `<foreignObject>` are stripped, as are `<style>` and `<a>`. An
inline `<style>` is not scoped to the icon, and an `<a>` would turn selecting the node into
a navigation. The attributes that survive are DOMPurify's SVG allow-list plus
`dominant-baseline` and `alignment-baseline`, so text can be centred the way Pivotick
centres its own glyphs. `<use>` is removed outright, so inline sprite symbols rather than
referencing them.

d282a52e3b8c7a6231f03461.source: `style.imagePath` is restricted to the `http:`, `https:`, `data:` and `blob:` schemes.

3b9fbb9c48e4f749d0cd677e.source:
Colours from the data, a node's `style.color` and a note's `color`, have to parse as CSS
colours before they reach the document, so they cannot smuggle a `url()` into a `background`.

639266fa442baa6fb3b53989.source:
Property values rendered as links carry `rel="noopener noreferrer"`, and any that leave your
origin, `//host/path` included, open in a new tab rather than replacing yours.

2b0daab26048c24e30c68421.source:
Earlier versions parsed such strings as HTML — property values in 1.3.0 and earlier, every other
`string | HTMLElement` option (extra panels, context-menu entries, custom renderers) up to 1.4.0.
If you were relying on that to inject markup, switch to returning an element.

92e83e377cbafdc0798e8f79.source:
A few options exist specifically so you can supply your own markup. Pivotick inserts what you
give it **verbatim**, so never build these from untrusted data:

7ce29fa5cfe28d27bfe5d4e0.source:
If you need data inside one of these, put it in with `textContent` on an element you created,
rather than interpolating it into a markup string:

b273d5498124b8304a2fcc37.source:
Nodes can reference pictures, via `style.imagePath` or an `<image href>` inside `style.svgIcon`.
Rendering such a node makes your users' browsers fetch that URL. If the URL came from untrusted
data, whoever wrote it learns that the graph was viewed, along with the viewer's IP address,
timing and `User-Agent` — a tracking pixel.

94f20ceffbc3555ec693d7fc.source:
Scheme restrictions can't prevent this, because `https:` has to be allowed for the feature to
work at all. If your data is untrusted and this matters to you, either strip/rewrite image
references before handing the data over, or constrain them with a Content-Security-Policy.

a909dd7fe99c6d7056c18bb2.source:
Pivotick needs no `eval` and no inline `<script>`, so it works under a strict policy. A CSP is
the cheapest way to blunt any injection — in the library, in your own code, or in another
dependency:

44ccec46914e4c4bf5358aaa.source: `script-src` without `'unsafe-inline'` is what neutralizes injected event handlers.

39c8b6b19084fd9b1ed331f5.source: `img-src` is where you pin down which hosts node pictures may come from.

55057dc6a0f454f4354837ec.source: `form-action` bounds where any injected form could post, whatever its `action` says.

be4eb42edb8eba3cc09479d4.source:
`style-src 'unsafe-inline'` is currently required: the renderer sets inline styles, and
Pivotick's stylesheet is normally injected by your bundler. Serve the CSS as a file and use a
nonce or hash if you need to drop it.

3bf19a74f09d3d418392dbe1.source:
Please report suspected vulnerabilities through
[GitHub security advisories](https://github.com/Pivotick/Pivotick/security/advisories) rather
than a public issue.

b66d8fe77b74ca9fef50405c.source:
Many graphs are mostly repetition. Two events share forty IPs, and each IP costs a node, a
label and two edges although what matters is "these two events share forty IPs". A hub has
dozens of leaves that link nowhere else. **Simplify** folds nodes that play the same role into
one **group**, drawn in their place:

5afefd4403a14905927e0291.source:
`graph.getNodes()`, `getEdges()`, the table, exports and the undo history see the real nodes.
A group is recomputed from them whenever the graph changes, and nothing about it is saved.

abc08699887984ad14de51af.source:
See it running on the [Simplify the graph](/examples/gallery/graph-simplification/content)
card.

f9121f51aa57dcaf4c60e805.source:
`UI.simplify.rules` is an ordered list. Each rule gives some nodes a key, and nodes sharing a
key become one group, as long as there are at least `minSize` of them.

74cb9da8aafceb81d40e0e29.source:
Rules run **in order**, and each one sees the groups the rules above it made as ordinary
nodes. A group can therefore be grouped again by a later rule.

e506be288455e7405d565fe9.source:
Rules run **after the node filters**, so a group only holds what passes them: hide three of
forty IPs and the group reads 37. Edge layers don't change groups; switching one off only
hides lines.

da2e0fe5fe77152a39b747e8.source:
A node with a note attached and an expanded cluster are **never grouped**. A closed cluster
groups like any other node.

2e402dd62738a5767f25086c.source: A declared rule is on unless it says `enabled: false`.

89ad5dd7f47f1f0977b1ec6f.source:
Without `UI.simplify`, `full` mode offers the built-in rules switched off in the Simplify rail
mode; the other modes run nothing. `UI.simplify.enabled: false` removes the feature.

12ef51708801422c1e752e56.source:
It folds nodes of **one type** that link to **exactly the same nodes, the same way round**:
the same nodes pointing at them and the same nodes they point at. The leaves of a hub are the
simplest case. With events A and B sharing three TTPs and each having two of its own, you get
three groups: the shared three between A and B, and two on each side.

835645f2b29b0d6151a35111.source:
The type is the rule's own `typeOf`, else [`UI.simplify.typeOf`](#types-and-colours-from-the-host),
else `render.nodeTypeAccessor`. Nodes with no type group among themselves.

7124bd6997127b5251345bd6.source: A node linked to nothing is never grouped: a group needs something to hang off.

09b3c517f282ca6ccef08626.source:
A node that gains a link leaves its group for the one that matches its new neighbours. If
that leaves fewer than `minSize`, the group dissolves.

24d004268fb80e7e1d64f848.source:
A group keeps its identity while it keeps most of its members, so a new node landing with the
same neighbours joins the existing group without moving it.

852a91c68ce8f2bd211efda3.source:
It folds chains that hang off one node. An event holding thirty files, each with its own hash,
is thirty chains `file > sha256`: the files share no neighbour, since each links its own hash,
so the neighbour rule leaves them alone. The chain rule folds them into one group of files
linked to one group of hashes, and draws the thirty links between them as one line.

5b975000b73284dac3acf565.source:
A node's **tail** is a node whose only link comes from it, followed downstream while each
step links only along the chain. A node linked from two others, a branch or a cycle ends the
chain there.

cc6fdc72e518789ce8a9f4e9.source:
Nodes that **lead chains of the same shape** fold together, when they share the same other
links and type. Five isolated pairs `domain → ip` give one group of five domains linked to one
group of five IPs.

c3a52450db15867a67b730bd.source:
**Each level** of the chains folds too: under the group of their heads, or under a head of
their own when it has no match.

748ff0ca1773736d13ccf2c9.source:
Links count **downstream only**: a node whose only link points at another isn't that node's
tail.

298f653acf24a48d26ee4407.source:
Placed after the neighbour rule, it folds what that rule left. A group the neighbour rule made
can be a tail.

aa14a730fa9e8e1a26ed0042.source:
These rules take nodes off the canvas by how well linked they are, and fold them into the
nodes they hang from, so the count stays on the canvas:

d7f144955cf4f8721ce5ec9f.source:
**Few links** (`degree`) folds nodes with fewer than `minDegree` links: at 2, a hub's leaves
become one group on the hub.

1726a26c1852a6c9f7d8c35f.source:
**Outside the core** (`kcore`) peels off nodes with fewer than `k` links, then does it again
with what is left, until every node standing has `k` links among the others. At 2 it folds
whole trees hanging off the graph, not only their leaves.

f92587c08e8f37be7fefe294.source:
Folded nodes that touch the same nodes left standing share a group, whatever their types, and
a group may hold a single node: it reads "1 more" on its anchor. Folded nodes linked together
go into the same group, so a path hanging off a hub folds with the hub's leaves. A run of
folded nodes touching nothing left standing is a group of its own, and every node linked to
nothing shares one group. Both settings go from 1 to 10, and links count either way round.

c34b58e64cb93525e14fac77.source:
After the neighbour rule, a group is one node to these rules: its links are its lines. A group
hanging alone off its anchor stays as it is.

5cc995804f7537b9a55e1fad.source:
For graphs too large for the rules above, Communities folds whole neighbourhoods: nodes more
densely linked to each other than to the rest of the graph become one group, whatever their
types. They are found with the Leiden algorithm, the same for the same graph every time.

f99e9d739dbe98525d204466.source:
`level` goes from **1, fine**, many small communities, to **7, coarse**, a handful of large
ones. In the Simplify mode it is a slider, applied when you let go.

14eeff3dd815df7ff52d3a0e.source:
The communities are found **in a worker**, off the page, and only again when the graph's
shape changes. Meanwhile the card reads *Grouping…* and the previous groups stay. Where no
worker can start, a Content Security Policy blocking blob workers for instance, the same code
runs on the page; `useWorker: false` asks for that.

732f38423e0c0980c576187c.source: A community of one node stays a node, and annotated nodes stay out, as for every rule.

77de085b9e2526ec4c66d09f.source: Unlike the other built-in rules, Communities is only in the Simplify mode when declared.

0daef36c2334d9bb816cdcb6.source:
*Ingest in a group*, in the [pivot](./pivots.md) Review pane's footer, lands the selected rows
folded: one group per type, hanging off the node you pivoted on. Forty IPs arrive as
"40 × ip" instead of forty dots.

f8a75c3a94d04b42c27901de.source:
A group holds what that ingest **added**. A node that was already on the canvas stays
where it was.

ddc828d41ff797f48c47d5a9.source:
A member **stays** whatever it links to later, unlike the neighbour rule. Pull it out, delete
it, or undo the ingest to take it out. Undo dissolves the group and redo brings it back.

250269b281bc9dd3d1029fb2.source: A type with fewer nodes than `minSize` (2 by default) lands as plain nodes.

5a9a2017e18d9b7d734a703b.source:
The rule runs first, so the rules after it see each landing as one node. You don't need to
declare it: the first grouped landing adds it at the top of the Simplify mode, switched on.
Declare it to put it somewhere else or change its smallest group.

037aba86c9eeb87b5a9f9895.source: Which landings are grouped lasts for the session, like open groups.

96ab54ef672fdd6c6ef0480f.source:
A landing group's `landing` names where it came from: `{ runId, pivotId, pivotLabel }`,
with the label from the pivot's definition. A chip can read `12 × ip · Event elements`
without parsing the run id.

82283a7de00a80816734187a.source:
To land every pivot result grouped, set `pivotIngestGrouped`. One-click runs and `autoIngest`
pivots, which never open Review, then land grouped too:

f97f50bcb9811471563a95fb.source: With `UI.simplify` switched off, the option does nothing and there is no second button.

7473be9bb95033363a0020ac.source: To choose for one ingest from code, pass `group`:

6fd0a3c06ff4a05b7e58c392.source: A rule of your own is a `partition(view)` returning a key per node:

096a31e6369bb3468924c42c.source: `view` is the graph as this rule sees it:

45da51d48f40c1ed93038af8.source:
A node left out of the map stays itself, and ids that are not in `view.nodes` are ignored. A
rule that throws is switched off, its card in the Simplify mode says so, and the other rules
still run.

309e1fb9a6bcdd64c6c383aa.source:
The **Simplify** button on the rail opens one card per rule, in run order: a switch, its
setting and what the rule folded. The setting is a − / + stepper for the smallest group, the
fewest links or the core strength, and a slider for the Communities level. Rules declared by
the app carry an *app* tag. The summary at the top reads how many nodes are on the canvas
out of how many pass the filters, and the rail button counts the groups while any rule folds.

d6b8e8778bf766c48a957da9.source: A group is drawn as a node, and it acts for its members wherever that is unambiguous.

489a56683c5025182e42d111.source:
**Open** it with a double-click, **Enter**, the sidebar or the context menu. Its members come
back as ordinary nodes, inside a wash in the group's colour, and a light pull keeps them
together. Drag the chip above them to move them all; its **×** folds them back. Its tooltip
names the rule that made the group. Members come back where they sat; those with no free
place of their own spread around the group, and live physics gets a gentle push, as for a
cluster. `simulation.fitViewOnExpandCollapse` fits the view on open and close. A group
with more members than `UI.simplify.openConfirmAbove` (100) asks first.

2b58f34764e3091b4d9a952d.source:
**Select** it to see its members in the sidebar, in a sortable list. *Pull out* keeps a
member out of the group until it is put back, from its context menu: on the canvas while
the group is open, or from its row in the data dock whether the group is open or not.
Over a selection it pulls out every selected member.

d61de4dff638b58ec5b0fd71.source:
**View in table**, in the sidebar or the context menu, lists the members in the data dock,
where the column filters narrow them further. The chip over the table lists every node again.

1d563b811e5040bbb230f206.source:
**Select members**, **Pivot** and **Delete** act on the members. Pivot and Delete go through
the usual hooks, so `onBeforeDelete` sees the real nodes. Hide, Delete and Pivot on a
selection that holds groups act on their members too.

0b04b2c2d3085ca3010d2438.source:
**Selecting a group** lights the nodes it links to, as selecting a node lights its
neighbours. Editing and connect-to are not offered on a group: it has no data of its own.

852717283d2e651c52492b0c.source:
Open groups and pulled-out nodes last for the session and are not undo steps. To restore
them, call `graph.simplify.open()` and `pullOut()`.

ad836c159110ba71d3c89ed8.source:
Select two nodes or more, then **Group** in the sidebar's bulk bar or *Group selected nodes*
in a selected node's context menu. Type a title, or keep the one offered ("3 × ip, 2 × domain"),
and the selection folds into one group under that title.

e8a15d2270d4fde24b44f235.source:
**A hand-made group wins.** Its rule, *By hand*, runs before every other, so a picked node
leaves any rule group. A selected group gives its members, and a node picked into a second
hand-made group leaves the first. Annotated nodes and open clusters stay out, and the
prompt says how many.

1c2a160124a37d72807ed2e0.source:
**It keeps its members** whatever they link to. One that is deleted or filtered out is not
drawn; a group left with one member is not drawn at all, and comes back with its members.

cc1731d9b25e4c6b1b2884c8.source:
**Rename** and **Ungroup** it from its sidebar panel or its context menu. An empty title
labels it by its types again. The bulk bar's **Ungroup** removes every hand-made group the
selection holds or sits in.

320aca4cb8bba837953af5e1.source: **Group, Rename and Ungroup are undo steps**, unlike opening or pulling out.

81fa79bcbb4f7da32836c037.source:
It is view state: not exported, and gone on reload. To keep it, save `getManualGroups()`
and hand it back to `setManualGroups()`. Groups restored, opened or pulled from right after
`new Graph()` are part of the opening layout: a closed group is placed as one dot, an open
one's members are kept together.

873cd57e1323b70dbee7bf60.source: Search looks through every node, the folded ones included.

3fc071c6850e106835be3e28.source: A match inside a group says so in its result row: *in 12 × ip*.

5e1681cd313f09d719a148f0.source:
Picking it opens the group and selects the node, as *Select members* would. A group with
more members than `openConfirmAbove` stays closed and is selected instead.

df43a520254adea46b528458.source:
**Show all on the canvas**, the last row of the results or **Shift+Enter**, closes the
search and lights every match; everything else fades. A group holding matches is lit too,
and an arc in the theme colour over its ring shows their share. Its tooltip counts them:
*2 of 12 match "198.51"*. **Esc**, a click on empty canvas or the next search ends it.

901232b049aea4f4770fc68b.source:
Hovering a legend entry marks groups the same way: a group holding nodes of that entry is lit,
with their share on its ring, so a group mixing types does not read as all of one.

f3feec850d30bccd48c371f6.source:
An app with a search of its own can mark its matches the same way with
`graph.simplify.setMatches(nodes, query)`, and clear them with `setMatches([])`.

41a180488a268a9a8c732aa8.source:
A group is a ring around a disc in its type's colour, with the count on the disc once there is
room for it and a label below. It grows with its count, up to a limit. A group mixing types
gets a neutral disc and a ring split by type.

dfe84447cf29a458a0a63b2c.source: The label is `12 × ip` by default. `typeLabel` names your types:

b7bc728f35ea0122983fda87.source:
`render.groupStyle(group)` returns a `NodeStyle` layered over the default, so `tiers`, `html`,
`shape` and badges work on a group as on a node. `render.groupOutline(group)` sets what the
chip over an open group says:

9c3287078eaca4ae27a64e85.source:
`groupStyle` also receives `base`, the style the library would draw. What you return replaces
its keys, so a host that adds a tier spreads `base.tiers` to keep the count on the disc:

d31140e4a96246c936e6c0a6.source:
The tooltip of a group names its rule, lists what it links to and, for a mixed group, its
members by type. `tooltip.renderGroupExtra(group, ctx)` adds your own lines, as
`renderNodeExtra` does for a node. A group skips `tooltip.render` and `renderNodeExtra`, which
are written for a node's data.

9b440d9cf2587a0e0b2fabbd.source: Types and colours from the host

26562f4504bae14010d111fa.source:
Groups count their parts by `render.nodeTypeAccessor` and colour them by each member's
style colour. Two `UI.simplify` options change that for every rule and group, without
touching styles, the legend or filters:

a76e53922a8be59e8440c431.source:
`typeOf(node)` is the type every rule groups by and every group counts its parts by: the
label, a mixed ring's shares, a hand-made group's title. A rule's own `typeOf` still wins
for that rule.

e9f845f4fd8d68dd50dd8ccc.source:
`colorOf(node)` is the colour a node stands for in a group: the disc and ring, the open
wash, the tooltip's chips. Returning `undefined` falls back to the node's style colour. A
group's own `groupStyle` still has the last word on the closed drawing.

9d6c24a06c7d499f4ba6d98b.source: A host that styles by element, groups by subtype and draws its nodes itself:

39921dca78346f9d73ca25ad.source:
The data dock lists the real nodes. A folded node reads `grouped` in the *Visibility* column,
and a *Group* column names its group while there are any. An edge whose line is drawn to a
group reads `grouped` too.

bb8f82978030ec7cb57f1ce5.source: `graph.simplify` holds the rules and the groups:

56bf919c2b70ecb189cd6584.source: Groups are a view, not data

027542aaab457c838f12db6e.source: The nodes this rule may group: what passes the filters, with earlier rules' groups in place of their members. Annotated nodes, pulled-out nodes and expanded clusters are left out.

d39b71c099680d3c8600f293.source: The drawn nodes with a line to, or from, this one.

f90da95fb3e3b27bad8cb92f.source: The type the rule groups by: `UI.simplify.typeOf`, else `render.nodeTypeAccessor`.

ec5782b2a364870b7b3204ea.source: The group behind a node, when it is one an earlier rule made.

89d733fb879aa811b35f751b.source: Stable while the group keeps most of its members.

531c814652682cec027eb92f.source: How many members of each type; `''` is no type.

52e6492ed115f78a67ed43b6.source: The drawn nodes it links to, groups included.

e43904c4800eada6e5a108fa.source: A landing group's run and pivot: `{ runId, pivotId, pivotLabel }`.

02b458d8dea866447c8b729b.source: Replace the rules; read each one's state and what it folded.

112a2382d39037b5991e8099.source: What the Simplify mode's switch and stepper do. `setRuleMinSize(id, n)` sets only a smallest group.

3a6c7eb7154ad27859998472.source: Every group, and the first group a node was folded into. A group a later rule folded again is listed too, beside the group holding it, and both list its members; `summary().groups` counts the closed groups the canvas draws.

f7f7da11a175454a0f82192d.source: Put a group's members on the canvas, or fold them back.

4e254599219685af54c7c040.source: Keep a node out of any group, or let it back.

49d56d00a0d4926b8aaa9e41.source: Make, retitle or remove [groups by hand](#groups-made-by-hand); each is an undo step.

6add2abda44acd71b074db05.source: Save the hand-made groups, and restore them.

f63df169b9ead9bc319d97b6.source: Fold what a pivot run adds into [landing groups](#pivot-landings), or draw it loose again.

c320071f360a3b87ad001ea5.source: How many nodes are drawn, pass the filters, and are folded.

02304bc30e5b1544c0432492.source: Mark a search's matches on the groups holding them; read how many a group holds.

8988e660aff910b710989cfe.source: Called after the grouping changes; returns its unsubscribe.

fc8a726575188c6c82beb709.source: In Pivotick, the physics simulation is partially managed for performance and stability. It includes:

e8043b3d69e026ec172b2c33.source: **Pre-computation**: the layout is simulated before the graph is rendered, stopping once it is nearly stable.

81257b09cf9bdadbec302828.source: **Timed execution**: the simulation automatically halts if it runs too long.

d9ac3ecc7ae458e0d2f2ee95.source: **Start/stop control**: the engine prevents the simulation from running unnecessarily in the background.

9e67dd038188fab353afde25.source:
Because of this controlled behavior, adding nodes after the simulation has finished will not automatically re-run the physics.
If you modify the graph dynamically, you'll need to manually "re-heat" the layout to trigger a new simulation pass.

949595c5e422106b63404375.source:
By default Pivotick tunes the layout for you. Rather than applying one fixed bundle
of force settings to every graph, it derives them from what is actually on screen —
how many nodes there are, how big they are, and how large the canvas is — and
re-derives them whenever that changes. Four small nodes get room to breathe; forty
large ones get packed closer without touching.

6dc20d43ff7857cc9db81650.source: This is the **Auto** preset, and it is on unless you say otherwise:

83dd6be877ea03056408104e.source:
The rule is deliberately conservative: setting **any** option that Auto drives
(`d3LinkDistance`, `d3ManyBodyStrength`, `d3CollideRadiusMultiplier`,
`d3VelocityDecay`, `d3GravityStrength`, `d3GravityStrengthConnected`,
`d3AlphaDecay`, `cooldownTime`) turns Auto off for that graph, so an existing
configuration is never quietly taken over. `physics: 'auto'` alongside explicit
options is still legal — the explicit values seed the opening frame and Auto takes
over from there.

7f3e1e7d9f32b3b9d51e9059.source:
Auto only ever moves the same knobs the Physics flyout exposes, and the sliders
follow along as it re-tunes, so its decisions are visible rather than hidden.
Turning any knob yourself — a slider, a `set*` call, or the Tight/Loose presets —
takes it back for good; nothing will re-tune over your choice afterwards.

e9689d0c16ea51bcb4e1fc37.source:
Auto is force-layout only. Under `tree` / `egoTree` it does nothing, because tree
spacing is the layout's own business.

9f1de20d96a55ef1de1445ed.source:
Auto never restarts a simulation that is paused (or that the slow-tick watchdog
switched off). It still works out the knobs; it just doesn't wake anything up.

c2e43cd53a8320b210726fb7.source:
Pinning `physics: 'manual'` is the right call for screenshot tests and thumbnails,
where you want the same picture every time regardless of graph size.

89192fad37d16126f45037e3.source:
† `'auto'` only for graphs that configure none of the options Auto drives; see
[Automatic layout tuning](#auto-physics).

38ffde74e592cbaead122490.source: Other D3 force parameters like `d3AlphaDecay`, `d3ManyBodyStrength`, `d3CollideRadius` are available and [documented in the API reference](/api/html/interfaces/SimulationOptions.SimulationOptions.html).

2c6b135d9d9a10041efd92c3.source: `onInit(sim: Simulation)`: Called when the simulation initializes.

71eaf72be2b7cb5d839e9623.source: `onStart(sim: Simulation)`: Called when the simulation starts running.

4e08e4b7f97cfd6075b0c7e9.source: `onStop(sim: Simulation)`: Called when the simulation stops.

dafd38aa9afa3b55686830d6.source: `onTick(sim: Simulation)`: Called on each simulation tick.

7ac90668795d75e7921fe8e8.source:
Pivotick exposes a simulation controller that lets you interact directly with the physics engine.
All methods are [available online](/api/html/interfaces/Simulation.html)

2dcb89aad781a10927ab765f.source: Should the initial node placement calculation done by a web worker

eccde3b95ff22fb27d8b619e.source: Who drives the force settings — see [Automatic layout tuning](#auto-physics).

31ccbeb07717502434c5b4a4.source: Ticks the opening layout runs before the first frame. `0` runs none, so nodes given an `x`/`y` open where they were, and auto physics re-tunes without moving them until the graph changes.

0efd21a62d7ccea76ef4338d.source: Minimum alpha value before the simulation stops.

40afde91b8b2951443dbb6af.source: Whether nodes are frozen once they are release from a drag operation.

7e551062fa4bc59844d717c4.source: Hooks for responding to simulation events.

d515af4e53bf880805b65752.source: The [context menu options](/api/html/interfaces/GraphUI.ContextMenu.html) configure right-click menus for nodes, edges, and the canvas.

1da3f9ec90ff42867cfe2f9e.source: Each menu (node, edge, canvas) have separate actions.

ac41c25c6f5bba67cf63ff21.source: Any additional custom actions are added after the default actions, above the delete.

eecb4a5b299bb01da365d35d.source: Pretty straightforward by setting the `enabled` property to `false`.

b5489dc6ce9ed942e968b7d9.source: You can customize the actions that appear when right-clicking a node, an edge, or the canvas.

76b2cb0b15f949d96e79816b.source: Each context menu is split into two sections:

4d8ebc2f4d659a3d0517f79b.source: `topbar` for quick actions (compact icons). Accept a [MenuQuickActionItemOptions](/api/html/types/GraphUI.MenuQuickActionItemOptions.html).

a079d4278e535c4a37a654fa.source: `menu` for full menu actions. Accepts a [MenuActionItemOptions](/api/html/types/GraphUI.MenuActionItemOptions.html).

b81fe370bbc87246e7e21e62.source: You can configure these menus for these scopes:

d8861fb487a62c604a766f85.source:
The node, selection and group menus read in the same order: **Pivot ▸** first, then the
[group](/simplify#working-with-a-group) entries that apply, then the other entries with
yours after them, and the delete last. A group's menu (Pivot · Open group · Select members ·
View members in table · Rename group · Ungroup · Select Neighbors · **Delete members**) is the
library's own and takes no entries of yours. An entry that doesn't apply is left out without
moving the others.

4c8044b096616699dd3687cf.source:
The write-path entries (delete, edit, create) go through their before-hooks — see
[Write-path lifecycle hooks](/callbacks#write-path-lifecycle-hooks) — and each disappears
when its `editors.<editor>.enabled` flag is `false`: **Delete** with `deletion`,
**Edit Edge** with `edgeEditor`, **Add Node Here** with `nodeCreator`, **Connect to…**
with `edgeCreator`. The same goes for entries that are a door into a switchable feature:
**Add Note** and the whole `menuNote` follow [`UI.notes`](/ui#turning-features-off),
**Inspect Properties** follows `UI.inspector`. Your own entries are never gated.
Both "…here" entries place their element where the **menu was opened**, whatever the
zoom or pan.

e1ea5eb1814876d6666fd388.source:
Right-clicking a node that is part of a selection of several nodes opens `menuSelection`,
headed with how many nodes it acts on. Every entry acts on the whole selection, as the
sidebar's bulk actions do, and the entries that only make sense for one node (Inspect,
Connect to…, View Image) are left out. Right-clicking a node outside the selection opens
that node's own menu and leaves the selection as it is, and the canvas keeps its own menu.
Entries of `menuSelection` receive the selected nodes as a `Node[]`, in `visible` as in
`onclick`.

8d44c51bf9d96f652d429255.source:
A row of the [data table](/ui-table#selecting) opens the same menu as its element on the
canvas.

d11d488d2d930c4a55375588.source:
**Del** hides the selected nodes. It hides rather than deletes because a hide costs
nothing to undo; **Delete Selected** is in the menu.

e1f2ec790f7a9aa4679b37f2.source: The interface for action items are defined [here](/api/html/types/GraphUI.MenuActionItemOptions.html).

983d8d0ada6bacac97ab456e.source: Pin / Unpin / Focus / Hide (topbar) · Pivot · Pull out of group · Put back in group · View Image · Select Neighbors · Hide Children · Connect to… · Inspect Properties · **Delete Node**

12be2de288a556099bba4d82.source: Pin / Unpin / Hide Selected (topbar) · Pivot · Group selected nodes · Pull out of group · Put back in group · Ungroup · Select Neighbors · **Delete Selected**

45932dd3e5338adcb59a01eb.source: Pin All / Unpin All (topbar) · **Add Node Here** · Add Note · Release pinned nodes (while any node is pinned)

498fcb6ca5028541252d1e2f.source: CSS class used as an icon. Typically used in icon libraries such as fontawesome. Example: `fa-solid fa-edit`

b261806015e964012860c08d.source: Unicode character used as an icon. Raw unicode to be used in icon libraries such as fontawesome. Example: `\uf007`

702924e631cf87871753d9d9.source: Path to an image used as an icon.

37cd7922d9514b49a43a159e.source: Inline SVG object used as an icon. Example: `<svg>...</svg>`

019d9fd46299302f863ca836.source: The action’s label shown in menus and toolbars.

20e25c22eabfff039095380d.source: Optional text label displayed next to the item.

a0dac4085a1d124556135487.source: Visual variant (style) of the menu item.

957bed226ef0d9460ef538c7.source: Controls whether the item is visible. Can be dynamic.

3860ad5ff10ba964872f393b.source: Triggered when the user activates the menu item.

7a19f0f2926edd5c1ea795da.source:
In `full` mode the header carries a **Graph Filters** panel (the funnel icon, or
**Shift+K**) whose form is built for you. By default the library derives that form
by scanning node data; `UI.filter` lets you take that over.

99a3cffdd3fc58c284efb8c1.source:
`UI.filter.enabled: false` removes the panel, its pill and **Shift+K** altogether;
`graph.queryEngine` still filters from code.

993b542124f359bb9b4e2c0a.source:
The form **applies itself**: a pick or a tick commits the moment you make it, a text or
pattern field a beat after you stop typing. There is no apply button, so the panel can
never be showing a filter the canvas hasn't got. **Reset**, beside the section label,
clears every attribute filter at once.

5a04a378314fc8b3585b35ed.source:
Everything on this page selects **nodes**. To filter *edges* — hiding a whole relation
kind without moving the graph — declare `UI.filter.edgeFacets` instead; they reuse the
same facet vocabulary and are documented under [Edge layers](/edge-layers).

d7bcf12fc54a4682b29f5b9a.source:
With no `UI.filter` at all, the panel walks every node's data keys, collects the
distinct values per key, and picks a widget from what it finds:

9e3d31ea0c602093bc1663ae.source:
Labels are prettified from the key (`attr-type` → *Attr Type*). This is a good
zero-config default for exploratory data, but it has no way of knowing which keys
are *facets* and which are internals — a `uuid` becomes a dropdown with one option
per node, and a long free-text field degrades to a text box.

d577d5420fa466c5df4896f0.source: The cheap fix when derivation is nearly right: drop the keys that are noise.

8d217a44e44a27b628e85db3.source:
Set `facets` and the form is generated from your declaration instead — exactly the
fields you list, in the order you list them, with your labels. Auto-derivation is
skipped entirely, so nothing churns as data changes.

fd56221eb84bcc584db68c7c.source:
A facet's `key` is also the key `queryEngine.setFilter(key, …)` uses, so
programmatic filtering and the panel stay on the same footing.

d0f0ae671e40af650b18a5d7.source:
**`regex`** — a pattern, compiled **case-insensitively**. An uncompilable pattern
is reported on the field and leaves the active filters untouched.

be8738180455c787528e39ef.source:
**`select`** / **`multiselect`** — pick from `options`. Pass an array, or a
function resolved against the live graph so option lists follow the data
without the facet set itself changing.

eb56a6c385658119f62ce5f6.source:
A declared `label` is used **verbatim**, so it can come from your translation
layer. Omit it and the key is prettified as in auto-derivation.

48297c77b0c56eddb09c44f2.source:
By default a facet reads `node.getData()[key]`. An `accessor` reads whatever you
like — including things that aren't on the node at all:

d5805d502fe3a2aeec4ea51e.source: Returning an array is fine — see [matching arrays](#matching-arrays) below.

57be3ff6dfbc2e171bfa64a9.source:
A `predicate` decides membership itself, and wins over `accessor` / `matchMode`.
It runs per node per filter application, so keep it cheap.

dbc4d5ea87c3114ecfd6cb1f.source:
A facet whose `accessor` or `predicate` throws stops matching (and warns once)
rather than taking the render down with it.

3c8fc47b2825cc323b01ad73.source:
Fields follow declaration order. Set `order` on a facet to place it explicitly —
handy when facets are assembled from several places.

d2b612f8987adac4dab57edc.source: `matchMode` decides how a filter value is compared:

71333587d2198c671794d2de.source:
**`'exact'`** <Badge type="warning" text="default" /> — strict equality. For a
multiselect (an array of picks) this is membership: any-of.

7dbd687554ad29e10c909e21.source: **`'all'`** — and-semantics: every selected value must be present.

2a744d26626c8a84825bad14.source:
When a node's value is an **array** — `data.tags = ['tlp:amber', 'malware']` — a
filter tests **membership**, not equality:

c0e581e140536d84b092efd3.source:
With `'partial'`, any single element may substring-match. A `numberRange` against
an array matches when any element falls inside the range.

1d0a458494556897d81e5b19.source:
Before this was supported, an array node value fell through to
`String(nodeValue).includes(value)` — so a filter for `malware` accidentally
matched a node tagged `not-malware`, and an array filter value never matched at
all. Both now behave as described above.

819b0a96eb3e61863dabae58.source:
`negate: true` keeps what the filter would otherwise hide. Each field in the panel has an
**is / is not** switch on its label row that sets it; a field switched to *is not* is drawn
red, its picks struck through.

94a5d0cd7d2a8ea9e6288936.source:
It reads the other way round for every widget: a list is *none of*, a text field
*doesn't contain* (with `'partial'`), a pattern *doesn't match*, a range *outside*. With
`'all'` it is *not all of*. A `predicate` facet's answer is inverted.

e7ee350ba264613465710bd4.source:
A node with **no value** for the key is kept, since it is not a domain either. So a filter
and its negation always split the graph in two, each node on exactly one side. A value
that narrows nothing (an empty list, a blank string, an open range, an unusable pattern)
still narrows nothing.

1da4bae6c07de398fa2cc6d1.source:
True / false fields have no switch: *is not true* is *is false*. Edge filters
(`setEdgeFilter`) take `negate` too. A [legend](/ui-legend) section that shares a facet's
key keeps a negated filter negated when you click it.

3715dfba9b8fbc5e68b8dce3.source:
Filtering relations away leaves nodes behind. Switch an
[edge layer](/edge-layers) off and a node whose only relation was in it stays on the
canvas with nothing attached — which is deliberate, because a layer is a lens. When you
*do* want those nodes gone, that is a node-side rule:

752dcbc9ee872681fad1dca3.source:
A node is hidden when it has no **visible** edge left, counted after the layers and the
node filters have had their say. A self-loop counts as a relation; a note pinned to a
node does not.

7492450164458cac85537be4.source:
The same switch is in the **View** flyout as *Hide unconnected*, on every graph, off
unless the option turns it on — so a user can clean up the orphans a layer toggle left,
or put back the ones you hid. While it is hiding, the row says how many.

14e47aaa7c87d179e8ca3986.source:
Everything else on this page, and every edge layer, leaves the layout alone. A hidden
node leaves the simulation, so the rest re-settle. That is the trade for a tidy canvas,
and it is why the rule is off by default.

a5cfe704d61f147bae56b943.source: Two things it deliberately does not do:

bff35e6fdd869117c2833315.source:
**Cluster interiors are left alone.** Clusters routinely group nodes with no relations
between them, so applying the rule inside one would open an empty box.

7499c9c2693bb1372a2871d2.source:
**Nothing is protected.** Switch off every layer and nothing is connected, so nothing
is drawn. The switch is the way back.

8c2a98a994980026d23c84e6.source:
Filters are applied when a filter changes — not when the graph's data does. Add the edge
a node was missing and it stays hidden until something recomputes:

827f80599b2f6a09c7d2e0f6.source:
Worth knowing before you call it: re-deriving visibility **undoes a manual
`graph.hideNode()`**, which nothing remembers. `queryEngine.excludeNode()` is the hide
that survives — it is what the context menu and the bulk actions use, and only *Show
node* reverses it.

2f5f3dfb951f102ad17bb9e1.source: Where the panel gets its values

e5a233bdc1e9f9c1df2abb21.source:
Filter *values* always flow through `graph.queryEngine`, whichever way the form is
built — so the header's active-filter count, the **Hidden nodes** list, and
propagation into an expanded cluster's subgraph all keep working. Declared facets
are handed down to a cluster's subgraph too, so an `accessor` / `predicate` facet
filters children exactly as it filters top-level nodes.

9d1669af99e5aecd7f0f9b9f.source:
The canvas [legend](/ui-legend) is a third way into the same engine: clicking a
legend row hides that category. Give the legend the `key` of a declared
`select` / `multiselect` facet and the two drive **one** filter, so the panel's
control and the legend stay in step.

128aa4cb31ba005977813c49.source:
The [data table](/ui-table#apply-to-graph) is a fourth: its **Apply to graph** button
hides the elements its column filters leave out. That push lands under a reserved key of
its own, so it survives anything this panel's form applies and is combined with whatever
this panel is filtering rather than replacing it. Because the form structurally cannot show a
reserved key, the panel grows a **From the table** row naming what the push is hiding —
and the only other place it can be cleared from, once the dock is folded away.

3be933c285d27a7960c4ec03.source:
See the [Filter / query engine](/examples/gallery/filter-query-engine/content)
gallery card for a live example, and
[`FilterFacet`](/api/html/interfaces/GraphQueryEngine.FilterFacet.html) for the
full type.

ec2404b08b487a5519d50c69.source:
`UI.legend` docks a **legend** in a canvas corner: one row per category, each with a
colour swatch, a label and the number of nodes behind it. Pointing at a row lights
that category on the canvas; clicking one hides it, so the legend doubles as the
fastest filter in the UI.

8011aeb18302788fe1cee199.source:
You may not need that block at all: with no `UI.legend`, a legend appears **on its
own** when your graph's colours are explained by a declared `render.nodeTypeAccessor`
— see [On by default](#on-by-default). `UI.legend: false` turns it off.

c8817a28b6394bcb7733ee94.source:
A graph that encodes several things at once needs several keys: pass `sections`
instead of a single key — see [Several keys at once](#sections).

a1d162b2a06c483aeaf51466.source:
The legend is part of the chrome, so it appears in `full` and `light` modes only —
`viewer` and `static` have none.

935c7f04912c7da8b3944812.source:
The legend is **descriptive**. It reads the colour the renderer already resolved for
a node (`renderer.getNodeStyle(node).color`) and reports it. Colouring stays where it
was: `render.defaultNodeStyle.color`, `render.nodeStyleMap`, or a per-node style —
typically via [`ColorPaletteMapper`](/examples/gallery/color-by-category/content).
Change the palette and the legend follows on its own.

3237df9893fee86c3d8e6411.source:
A legend is only worth showing unasked if it is guaranteed to tell the truth, so the
automatic one starts from something you already declared rather than from a guess
about your data: **`render.nodeTypeAccessor`**, the dimension you point
[`nodeStyleMap`](/render) at.

902b7a7ac7a51c4e9fe82687.source:
Having a candidate isn't enough, though — a dimension can partition your data without
having anything to do with its colours. So before rendering anything, the legend
checks that this dimension **explains the colours**:

5b4d26d0a0db122e4a5e3b5a.source: every category resolves to exactly **one** colour;

c9c2eab079da3ce6f210d058.source:
there are at least **two** distinct colours (otherwise the colours aren't telling
the categories apart);

f8b121a9a64f77477c825900.source:
there are at most **24** categories — an id-like dimension yields one value per
node, each with its own colour, which would otherwise sail through the check above.

cfcd21fc59a56dd10c44b21f.source:
If any of that fails, no legend appears and nothing is logged: you didn't ask for one.
The automatic legend is also skipped past **5000 nodes**, where sampling every node's
colour isn't worth paying for uninvited — that one warns, so the absence is
explainable. Declaring `UI.legend` (or `true`) lifts both.

7316b7c15f0e7ce29091f7c4.source:
An automatic legend keys on an accessor rather than a data key, so it can't
[share a filter](#sharing-a-filter-with-the-panel) with a declared facet — give it an
explicit `key` for that.

b35484aef6ed4a99a4428084.source:
`key` is the whole configuration in the common case: the distinct values of
`node.getData()[key]` become the rows, in first-seen order, labelled with the value
itself.

274bab6d159ac401ae0b1b16.source:
An **array-valued** key contributes one row per element, and a node counts under
each of them (`tags: ['public', 'critical']` appears under both).

ff78b39f61ba3f562c73b7ec.source: Two things are worth knowing about derived rows:

c6408f2af6d64c65a872f443.source:
**Nodes with no value** for the key (`null`, `undefined`, `''`) get no row, and the
legend can never hide them — it only acts on the categories it lists. A dev-time
warning names the key and how many nodes are unrepresented.

aae0c22b23bb1c866932406a.source:
**A category painted in more than one colour** keeps the first colour found, with a
warning: one row can only show one swatch. Declare the entries yourself if the
grouping isn't really one colour.

9c9d2b127657c73759ec654e.source:
Pass `entries` when the categories aren't a plain data key — computed groupings,
translated labels, a fixed colour scale. Each entry carries its own `predicate`,
which is what the toggle filters on.

a413657580017d70e323e56f.source:
`entries` may also be a **function** of the graph, re-resolved whenever the data
changes — so the list follows the data without the declaration churning:

fab82c7729129afa577d3c51.source:
Declaring both `entries` and `key` is the useful middle ground shown above: the
entries give the labels and colours, and `key` supplies the default predicate
(`data[key] === id`) for entries that don't carry one. An entry with neither warns
and matches nothing.

1a9009a04d8479c763851183.source:
A row's toggle state survives a re-resolution; an entry that disappears from the data
loses it rather than lingering as a hidden ghost.

4b4821b24f0175656e945faa.source:
A graph that encodes three things — kind in the fill, provenance in the enclosure,
relationship in the stroke — needs three keys, not one. Pass `sections` and each gets
its own titled block, stacked top to bottom in **declaration order** inside one docked
card:

3d9fe52bf8ed2059e5c9946d.source:
A section takes everything a single legend takes except `position`, which belongs to
the card. Sections are independent in every other way: their own entries, their own
counts, their own fold state, their own filter.

f7617040ca3e2b28a1d1291d.source:
Each filterable section drives **its own filter**, and the query engine ands them:
switch `attribute` off in the first section and `self` off in the second, and what
stays on the canvas is the nodes that are **neither**. Every section's `show all`
clears only that section.

77d6eedc0a53826466992609.source:
A section writes to `__legend:<id>`, where the id is the section's `id`, else its
`key`, else its place in the stack (`section-0`). A **single-key** legend — the object
form — keeps the plain `__legend` it has always used. As with a lone legend, a section
whose `key` names a declared `select` / `multiselect` facet
[drives that facet](#sharing-a-filter-with-the-panel) instead, and its siblings are
unaffected.

adf4f3cf6247aa36776f12ae.source:
A section declaring `scope: 'edge'` lists the graph's **relation kinds** with a *line*
swatch — stroke colour, dash and marker as the renderer resolved them — and its toggles
hide edge layers rather than nodes. It sits beside node-scoped sections in the same card
and leaves them untouched. See [Edge layers](/edge-layers#legend) for the whole feature.

faba669ce835c36c3a687966.source: Naming the dimension you style by

432428532d181e49d26e1fef.source:
A section with neither `key` nor `entries` is the dimension you already declared as
`render.nodeTypeAccessor` — the one spelling for a styling dimension that isn't a
plain data key. It skips the [colour check](#on-by-default): inside a `sections` list
you asked for it. Only one section may do this; a second is dropped with a warning.

2bd582b6856e7ad44b59eae4.source:
Swatches are **sampled from the colours the renderer resolved**, and that is the only
channel the legend can read. A section keyed on a dimension the colours don't encode
— provenance, when provenance is drawn as an enclosure — gets the colour of the first
node in each category, and warns that the category renders more than one. Declare
`entries` with your own `color` on that section to give it swatches that mean
something.

d6011da3dc9e86effdd54659.source:
Sections fold individually; **alt**-click any chevron to fold or unfold the whole
stack at once. Each section still scrolls its own list past `maxVisibleEntries`, and
the card as a whole is capped against the canvas height and scrolls rather than
growing past it — so six sections stay inside the viewport.

3cf4cd9528471238527392b0.source:
A section that resolves to **no entries** (a key no node carries, an empty
declaration) is skipped entirely rather than shown as an empty titled box; a card
whose sections are all empty renders nothing at all.

421cc4dc272dd6f751c58405.source:
Point at a row and the canvas answers: the elements that category stands for keep the
look they have, everything else dims until the pointer leaves. Nothing is filtered and
nothing moves, so it is the cheap way to find where a category sits before deciding
whether to switch it off.

e1b30ae70b82c0c85e0702c5.source:
A row on a [`scope: 'edge'`](#keying-edges-instead-of-nodes) section lights its
**lines**, with the nodes receding along with the other layers. An edge folded into a
closed cluster or a [simplify](simplify.md) group lights the line drawn in its place.

02b8197dbd43226aea62219b.source:
Pointing at a category that is already switched off dims nothing — there is nothing
left on the canvas for it to light.

669fe97bfe1ed07f3b14e771.source:
`highlightOnHover: false` turns it off for a section. A `filterable: false` key
highlights too, where it is the only thing a row does.

768f8d96f5e51311f6d1d354.source: The same set can be lit from code, and holds until it is cleared:

224834a324d56469e9640dab.source:
Both take the elements the renderer drew, so they read `getMutableNodes()` /
`getMutableEdges()` rather than the cloning getters.

701358ad442a8353b75b7000.source:
Toggling a row writes a filter to `graph.queryEngine` — the same engine the
[filter panel](/ui-filter) drives — so nothing about it is a second, parallel
mechanism:

eee427f35d841bc6d945c5e7.source: Nodes added **after** a toggle, in a hidden category, arrive hidden.

58bbe6d3318d043ea3df94b5.source: A hidden category stays hidden inside an expanded cluster's subgraph.

940f73afd6df6db1fce5fb45.source: `resetFilters()`, or the panel's **Reset**, re-lights every row.

397d00c4990316f61113129b.source:
With every row shown the filter is *removed*, so the header's active-filter count
doesn't report a legend that isn't hiding anything.

a237489941f62b85d5697f5c.source:
By default the legend owns a reserved filter key of its own (`__legend`) matched
through a predicate — one per section, namespaced as `__legend:<id>`, in the
[stacked form](#sections).

4b6cdc8fd8b849f087a67444.source: Sharing a filter with the panel

5138a25553b67ac095d598e8.source:
When `key` names a declared `select` / `multiselect`
[facet](/ui-filter#declared-facets), the legend drives **that facet's key** instead.
The legend and the panel then become two views of one filter: switch a swatch off and
the panel's multiselect drops that value; pick values in the panel and the legend
re-lights accordingly.

b550f627bfc65feca548268b.source: Two consequences of speaking the panel's language:

cc903120656b3fc2de584505.source:
An **empty** multiselect means *no constraint* to the panel, so the legend can't
express "hide everything": the last shown row is disabled rather than writing a
value that would bring the whole graph back. A legend on its own key has no such
limit.

09ca314589460024d817a8b7.source:
Nodes with **no value** for the key are hidden by any selection, exactly as they are
when you filter from the panel.

f25fa4dddb06c104cb316076.source:
If `key` names a facet of another type (`text`, `regex`, `numberRange`, `boolean`) the
legend keeps its own key and warns — a value list has no meaning there.

476ad596116c8b58a23e001c.source: Every toggle is announced on the [data event bus](/callbacks):

08fa912a14a1471b357b5015.source:
`section` is the id of the section that was toggled, and `hidden` / `visible` are that
section's rows. A single-key legend reports its own derived id (its `key`, else
`section-0`).

e0a5882c94ceadd23870b1ef.source: Restoring is the same call the legend makes:

e69321a894396e63e7315c7d.source:
`graph.setLegend(config)` replaces `UI.legend` live. A graph that started without a
legend gets one built on the spot, and `false` removes it — clearing its filter with
it, so nothing stays hidden behind a legend that is gone.

c91d0c0736d9ab95ca0b2a68.source:
Swapping between the two forms renames the filter keys, so the filters of the form you
left are dropped: nothing stays hidden behind a section that is gone.

ec2afce5304824db8856a72b.source:
`UI.legend` also takes a **boolean**: `false` suppresses the legend, `true` derives one
from `render.nodeTypeAccessor` without vetting the colours first. Everything below is
the object form.

ef8b2e51f4369445f153fd6c.source:
The **stacked** form is `{ enabled?, position?, sections }`: `sections` is the list
below minus `position`, and `enabled` / `position` describe the whole card.

12ef075eddb74d6db03e50ff.source:
A `LegendEntry` is `{ id, label?, color, badge?, predicate?, order? }`. `id` is the row's
identity, the value written to the filter, and the label's fallback.

6803043cd2480cd8cd2aaafd.source:
When nodes are told apart by a [badge](/render#node-badges) rather than by their fill, give
the entry that `badge` and the row shows the mark instead of a dot. It is drawn the way the
canvas draws it, and a badge naming no `color` takes the entry's. Filtering is unchanged.

bfb1ba764b6b95fae0369768.source: `maxVisibleEntries` is one ceiling on the legend's height; the canvas is the other.

fcd0105529dc9eef2f225e26.source:
In `full` mode the legend docks bottom-right by default, stacking above the minimap
that mode also mounts: the left column belongs to the mode rail and its panels, and a
rail mode whose panel is a workspace rather than a settings sheet reaches far enough
down it to leave the legend a single row. Where a minimap shares the chosen corner the
legend sits on top of it, following it as it collapses, resizes or unmounts.

08b25bc9b005b5f08cd85052.source:
A `bottom-left` legend shares its column with the mode rail, so on a short viewport it
shrinks to the room between them and scrolls at whatever row that lands on, rather
than growing up under the rail. It never moves corner on its own.

b45f97e273f812badc9b9822.source:
Rows are real buttons: tab-reachable, `Enter` / `Space` toggle, and `aria-pressed`
carries the state. A hidden row is drawn with a hollow swatch **and** dimmed text, so
colour is never the only signal.

078f9ddd299df9cd7de0c4d1.source:
See the [Filterable legend](/examples/gallery/filterable-legend/content) gallery card
for a live example, and
[`LegendOptions`](/api/html/interfaces/GraphUI.LegendOptions.html) /
[`LegendGroupOptions`](/api/html/interfaces/GraphUI.LegendGroupOptions.html) for the
full types.

4c158ddad4b6abba37784aac.source: A section keyed off the colour dimension

febad1b46ce8654b397bc9d6.source: `false` keeps the declaration but shows nothing (same as `legend: false`).

8dcb0188f6950738b5570ae8.source: Section identity: its filter key (`__legend:<id>`) and the `legendToggle` `section` field.

784fae2ed3ae909eb6460378.source: Data key the rows are derived from, and the default predicate for declared entries. Omit both this and `entries` for the [automatic](#on-by-default) legend.

28bf4b5b50fc6347f7852708.source: Declared rows; a function is re-resolved on data change.

716596dec305735f0d8e2ec8.source: Which canvas corner it docks in. Belongs to the card, so it is **not** a section option. `'top-left'` shares its anchor with the contextual tool panel, which covers the legend while open.

dbc544b9942755ef20ed3e84.source: Show the chevron that folds it to its title.

4097d63ddf7fbe766ca27dc2.source: Show the per-category node count (over the whole graph, so it doesn't flicker as you toggle).

53e87b31966ae6c35043d2c3.source: Hovering a row lights that category on the canvas and dims the rest.

8f9a7f79b8c01dc3e9605324.source: Rows shown before the list scrolls inside the legend.

3b00dd781639590144f0b0d3.source: Light that category on the canvas, dim everything else

4c15397f6e538964eb5cf549.source: Re-light every row (clears the legend's filter)

fc98843e60f9b01dad997bdd.source: Fold that section to its title

90e3e84523c8ed857833cfb4.source: Fold or unfold every section at once

23a2dcb686705fdad3bf52ec.source: The sidebar can be collapsed by default depending on screen size or user preference.

634ab63d9637aca4c6c1b08d.source: `'auto'` <Badge type="warning" text="default" />: Keeps the sidebar open unless there isn't enough screen space, in which case it collapses automatically.

f4284da424854e99ecfc535f.source: The sidebar displays contextual information for graph elements. It has three customizable components:

e0a67634e8cfb6f0782da7d8.source:
`UI.sidebar.enabled: false` drops the whole column and hands its width back to the canvas.
The properties and neighbours panels have a switch each — `UI.propertiesPanel.enabled`,
`UI.neighborsPanel.enabled` — which removes that panel and its separator while the rest of
the sidebar stays. See [Turning features off](/ui#turning-features-off).

ce55879319924a308e1fd08e.source: Shows a concise summary of the selected node or edge, such as title and subtitle. It helps users quickly identify the current selected element.

939f4d171a13214d0a63b410.source: The main header panel can be customized through mapping functions. The default mapping for a node is

43c7c60a8c51479a0de15578.source: You can change this mapping by overriding the parts you need:

a5c6c02f53142eca6c72a668.source: When `render()` is provided, Pivotick skips all default mapping logic, unless it returns `undefined`. An `undefined` result (or a promise resolving to `undefined`) draws the default header for that selection: the `nodeHeaderMap` / `edgeHeaderMap` title for one element, the selection count for several, and the canvas total when nothing is selected. Return `null` to leave the header empty.

d877d738acc5334ff611c61b.source: Displays detailed properties of the selected node or edge in the sidebar. Each property has a name and value that can be static or computed dynamically.

6ed59991152185ad7ab7ddb5.source: The default behavior is to show all key/value pairs from the node or edge's [`getData()`](/api/html/classes/Node.html#getdata).

f23c87942611fc09d6ad11f6.source: You can customize which properties are displayed and how they are rendered using mapping functions (`nodePropertiesMap` and `edgePropertiesMap`) or a full custom renderer.

4b8fca89a46e75dc3dbcefc0.source: A properties map may return several entries with the same name, such as one `Tag` entry per tag. In a multi-selection each value then counts the nodes carrying it, keep/exclude matches any of a node's entries, and each value gets its own bar, since the values overlap.

dfe5c56fd8d5a989d68df71c.source: When `render()` is provided, Pivotick skips all default mapping logic, unless it returns `undefined`. An `undefined` result (or a promise resolving to `undefined`) draws the default panel for that selection: the `nodePropertiesMap` / `edgePropertiesMap` rows for one element, and the aggregated table, with its keep/exclude filters, for several. Return `null` to leave the panel empty.

bf2026d4463ae12c64a1a148.source: Shows the selected node's connections: a small graph of its neighbours, connection stats, and a list.

7bc3c306eee92b8516cd655e.source: The neighbour graph draws with the main graph's render options by default. Styles that suit a full canvas, such as node detail tiers or a focus card, can crowd a panel this size, so `graph` takes overrides of its own:

290f08191ae2d07eb29e32da.source: `graph.render` is merged over the main graph's render options. The panel's own settings (no drag, no zoom, no node expansion) still apply. A `maxZoom` here also caps how far the graph zooms in to fit, so a node with one neighbour is not blown up.

e1baece469124c9a22da0999.source: `graph.layout` is merged over the panel's radial layout. The root is always the selected node.

6540398882fc36631fcee206.source: Allows adding fully custom panels with dynamic or static content. These panels are ideal for showing additional contextual information, custom controls, or interactive widgets related to the selected element.

00e51feecff8c99de60ced76.source: Each extra panel has an optional `title` and a `render()`, both of which can be static (string/HTMLElement) or a function of the current selection. A returned `string` renders as **text**; return an `HTMLElement` to render your own markup. Return `null` to leave the panel body empty.

a9aa62ce905df90660cd64a6.source: The selection a panel is rendered with

b0e781b135e120f2b46a8451.source: `title` and `render` are re-invoked on **every selection change**, with what is currently selected:

45df442dd7da105f15b7379a.source: A panel is only *shown* while something is selected, unless it sets `alwaysVisible: true` — but a reactive panel is re-rendered either way, so it never holds content describing a stale selection.

c414c791f473d47119a6464f.source: Set `reactive: false` for a panel that doesn't describe the selection and is expensive to build: it then renders once, and only an explicit `refreshPanel()` rebuilds it.

77ed1ff5141eb36d80357283.source: `UI.extraPanels` is the declarative form of the same registry. Anything you can declare there you can also register — and remove — at any point in the graph's life, through the [`UIManager`](/api/html/classes/UIManager.html):

55e480e8b88b937906c0f428.source: Panels sort by `order` (ascending, default `0`) and keep registration order within the same value, so `UI.extraPanels` reads top-to-bottom and runtime panels append after them.

94a136056d6ab226636f7947.source: A panel's own `title` / `render` receives a second argument — a handle on itself — so it can drive its own updates without reaching for the graph:

1ef669aa16e642b91c67ddbc.source: Panels are shown by the sidebar, which exists in `full` mode. Registration succeeds in any mode — the panel simply has nowhere to render until a sidebar does.

190b71be1326cba9e64d7d1b.source:
`title` and `render` may both be `async`, as may the properties panel's
`render` / `nodePropertiesMap` / `edgePropertiesMap` and the main header's
`render`. The panel shows a placeholder while the promise is pending:

5551c2cb3e287f7d343dd4e3.source:
Note the argument order: the panel handle stays second, and the
[`RenderContext`](/api/html/interfaces/AsyncContent.RenderContext.html) is
always **last**.

2d6480b5fcc1da1680c96aa1.source:
Because a panel re-renders on every selection change, a fetch is routinely
superseded before it resolves. The library handles that for you: the old
render's `signal` is aborted, and a result arriving after the selection moved on
is dropped rather than painted into a panel describing a different node. The
same applies to `refreshPanel()` and to removing the panel. See
[asynchronous content](./ui#async-content) for the full contract.

709cf55fd8dbf783041c621d.source: Register a panel; returns a disposer. `id` is auto-generated when omitted. Works before and after the graph is ready, and from a plugin's `install` (as `ctx.addPanel`).

4d0d896102458c6efebd2dda.source: Remove the panel and its DOM.

ffb74764734c56eaaa1516f5.source: Re-render one panel, or all of them. Refreshes `reactive: false` panels too.

c655c02ae66661d0829d9d81.source: The registered panels, in display order.

df0ddcff2d80b0e2e30e795c.source: `.pivotick` – The main container for the pivotick UI.

7b10d27099814e8c4689b1b7.source: `.pvt-sidebar` – Left panel for the current selection (properties, facets, neighbours) and bulk actions.

10c7fdbfe414dbdc1789637c.source: `.pvt-canvas` – The area where the graph is rendered.

3a751b1f9ed010dfc001766c.source: `.pvt-moderail` – Left mode rail (Select / Create / View / Physics).

b4d144375167d9a45157e08c.source: `.pvt-toolpanel` – Contextual tool panel for the active mode.

8bdf685fb45a3416997231e0.source:
`.pvt-flyout` – Slot holding the settings flyouts; each panel is a `.pvt-flyout-panel`
(`.pvt-flyout-view` for grid / canvas switches, `.pvt-flyout-physics` for layout and simulation).

18552dd4ece55019ed880c96.source: `.pvt-tooltip` – Tooltip container for nodes or edges.

11ea6dbfb441609798a5357e.source: `.pvt-contextmenu` – Context menu container for right-click actions.

faeb8a8391e61f773574979b.source: `path` – The SVG path representing the edge.

c31519fe1dc59b8f13b1a45c.source: These are the core classes you can override. To see all available classes, just open your browser's developer tools and inspect the element.

c40138764b8772dba6c0d3a6.source: Another easy way to style Pivotick is to override the default CSS variables. You can find them all [here](https://github.com/Pivotick/Pivotick/blob/main/src/styles/_variables.scss).

acb1d271dbb14f30c2c4e558.source:
`UI.table` splits a **data dock** off the bottom of the canvas: the graph's nodes and
edges as a sortable, selectable grid. It exists because a force layout is structurally
bad at three things people do constantly — reading exact values, selecting at scale, and
working out where to start.

5c9eb8462c2a8b5f326f36b1.source:
The intended loop is **table to find, canvas to understand, sidebar to read**: sort by
degree to spot the hubs, shift-click the top twenty, and act on them with the sidebar's
bulk actions.

ae39cde9678a22eceb1df2d9.source:
That is all it takes. In `full` mode the dock sits at the bottom **folded to its header
bar**; click its chevron — or press `Shift+T` — to show the table. `UI.table: false`
removes it entirely.

5a0d08b4f4fbfb2cf04eb6b6.source:
There is deliberately no toolbar button for it. The bar *is* the control: the pills in the
top bar all open something *over* the canvas, while the dock is a split region that already
shows you its own chevron.

5b9899b5ec57a16b338cd7c3.source:
The dock is `full` mode only — it is a grid row beside the sidebar, and the other modes
promise a canvas without that much chrome.

349c750b572e8daa8bda7091.source:
The dock mutates nothing. It reflects the graph and drives the selection; hiding and
pinning stay with the sidebar's [bulk actions](/ui-sidebar), and restoring a hidden node
stays with the [filter panel](/ui-filter). What the dock adds is a far better instrument
for *building* the selection those act on.

3bdcedf7a0d942f9074ab444.source:
The one thing it can change is what the canvas **shows**, and only on request: the
[Apply to graph](#apply-to-graph) button hides the elements your column filters leave out.
Until you press it, narrowing a column is reading, not filtering.

47321cdfa8583a22b97b934d.source:
The table does **not** mirror the canvas. It lists every node — and on the Edges tab every
edge — including the ones currently hidden, and the leading `Visibility` column says where
each one stands:

65032fb48b5768cff85a9a34.source:
Each state differs in weight and border as well as colour, so the column reads without
relying on hue. A hidden element's whole row also recedes, keeping the eye on what is
actually drawn.

14f3016d6402f86523d07760.source:
An edge reads `endpoint` in preference to `filtered`, because that is the reason you have
to fix first: while a node it touches is gone, switching its layer back on cannot bring
the edge back.

79d4e00f498db90298f4ab22.source:
That is deliberate. "23 nodes hidden" is a claim you should be able to inspect, and a
table that quietly drops the rows you are looking for is worse than no table. Sort by
`Visibility` to see exactly what a filter took away.

90bd60186bd763d4fa3f572d.source:
A cluster's contents get rows too, as **peers** of the graph's own nodes, with
a **Cluster** column giving the path they came from (`Team B / Squad`, outermost first) and
a **Children** column saying how big each cluster is. Both columns appear whenever the
graph has clusters. The header's **Nested nodes** switch takes those rows out again if you
only want the top level, and `UI.table.nested: false` never offers them at all.

d79fdf69001e6156d71628a0.source:
They are listed flat rather than indented under their cluster on purpose: the table exists
to answer questions the canvas cannot — which nodes are the hubs, which are over a
threshold — and that only keeps working if a sort or a filter reaches every row equally. A
tree can only ever sort siblings.

0beb7c118607fa079905bf79.source:
What is worth knowing is that a nested node is **not drawn by this graph**. An open cluster
renders a separate subgraph of its own, so:

93e9e7cdd89fcdcef6c22ba5.source:
`Visibility` reads `nested` while any cluster above the node is shut, and `visible` once
they are all open. It is never `filtered` — no filter put it there.

6e56a9936951ff1c62d62dec.source:
`Degree` counts the node's real edges. While its cluster is shut the canvas draws them
to the cluster instead, so this is the node's own count rather than a description of
the picture.

604600bf7b4c25b789171026.source:
Clicking the row selects the node, so the sidebar can show it — often the only way to
reach it. The canvas rings the closed cluster that stands for it. **Double-clicking
opens that cluster**, one level per press. With `render.enableNodeExpansion: false` the
cluster stays shut and the view centres on it instead.

bd30922535df2d695f7583d1.source:
Click any column heading to sort; click again to reverse. Filterable columns grow a
control in the header that **narrows the rows** — every column in the
[derived set](#columns) has one, and a column you declare yourself gets one by asking for
`filterable: true`.

2ccd4acfa68c2cd3793b635b.source:
Which control you get follows the column's `type`, so you can ask a column what it is
actually able to answer:

74403684ac3001ef9dd9835c.source:
The dropdown is built from the column's own values rather than a declared option list, so
it never offers a choice that would come back empty. Above 50 distinct values it steps
aside for the text box — a dropdown that long is not a control anyone can use.

d487f929e14a7ed589ce1b7c.source:
A row filter is not the graph's filter. It changes what you are *reading*: the canvas is
untouched and the `Visibility` column goes on reporting the truth beside it, so the two can
disagree without either being wrong. Pushing your narrowing onto the canvas is a separate
and explicit act — see below.

7da6f323a89980565d2f0582.source: The dock's count reflects both: `40 nodes` becomes `12 of 40 nodes` once you narrow.

e233d816bdb5eba0c704b655.source: Applying the filters to the graph {#apply-to-graph}

966a1f0ed2a04743a7d4246f.source:
**Apply to graph**, in the dock's toolbar, hides the elements your column filters leave
out. It is the bridge between the two kinds of filtering: narrow the rows until the table
lists what you care about, then press it once and the canvas shows the same thing.

45d5c09be3fed6a54b791b9a.source:
It is a one-shot push, not a live link, and the button says which of three states you are
in:

784466e822ab842998825725.source: Two properties worth knowing, because they are what keep the push predictable:

c3e027a00eab517e09d70822.source:
It hides **exactly the rows the filters left out** — never "show only these". So a node
added after the push stays on the canvas. What you pushed is a statement about a moment,
not a standing query. An open cluster's interior narrows only in so far as its own rows
were among the ones left out; with [nested rows](#nested) switched off, nothing names
them and the interior is untouched.

0e3c55354accc72b935891d1.source:
The `Visibility` column is **never** part of a push, though it still narrows rows like
any other. Its values *are* the graph's filter state, so pushing them would hide whatever
is currently on the canvas and then disagree with itself.

2afe36a38208777c3cdce605.source:
While a push is live the count reports both halves — `12 of 40 nodes · 28 hidden` — and the
[filter panel](/ui-filter) grows a **From the table** row that names it and can clear it,
so a push is never a filter you cannot find once the dock is folded away.

54e5c84589eed7e0e5666433.source:
The push lands as a single filter under a reserved key, which means it composes with the
filter panel rather than competing with it: nothing you set in that panel's own form ever
clobbers a push, and a push never clears the panel's filters. The two are combined, so a
node has to survive both.

c9df6de2f8d70df3c2956d21.source: Pass `filterGraph: false` for a dock whose controls can never touch the canvas at all:

710955058f6a0cf1228bf99e.source:
It works in both directions: rubber-band a group on the canvas and the matching rows are
marked and scrolled to. The selection is the same one the sidebar's bulk actions read, so
the loop closes without any extra wiring.

e1ee3d34db918b35894fc000.source: Hidden rows select like any other — that is the point of listing them.

dffe37ad87457648bf9465b0.source: With no `columns` declared, the dock works it out for you, in three tiers:

25afb49a1c3b87ba50d0d2bc.source:
**From your facets** — otherwise, if you declared
[`UI.filter.facets`](/ui-filter#facets), columns are built from them. Describe your
data once and the filter panel and the table agree about it.

01e8b172d6821bbacfccdb3d.source:
**Scanned** — otherwise the data is read, ordered by **coverage** so the
well-populated keys come first and the sparse tail sits at the far right.

6bbe3d7bc387d0220dae7ffb.source:
Either way the graph-aware columns wrap the data. For nodes, **`Visibility`** and
**`Label`** lead — a status gutter and the name, the two things you scan down to find a
row — joined by **`Cluster`** on a graph that has clusters, since a
[nested row](#nested) needs it to say where it came from. The counts close it:
**`Degree`**, plus **`Children`** on a graph that has clusters. The counts sit at the end
because they are the graph's arithmetic rather than
the element's own data, and they are narrow, fixed-width columns so a couple of digits
never take the share of the row a name needs. Edges keep the same `Visibility` gutter and
then read as a sentence — `Source` / `Label` / `Target`.

a191a25c73ff2d64c5ca86b1.source:
The default sort is the `Label` column, not the leading one: sorting by `Visibility` on
open tells you nothing while every row still reads `visible`.

2b47b057ead577d9682bacfd.source:
Everything is shown by default, and the grid scrolls sideways rather than dropping
